heading: Snow walls, hemp blocks and sea ice
intro: This lab asks how energy moves from hotter to colder, and how insulation slows it down. Inuit, Plains Cree and Métis governments, businesses and builders are working with heat transfer every day, from iglu walls to hemp building blocks to sensors that measure warming sea ice. These connections name the people doing that work and cite a source for every fact.

connections.title: A Métis government slowing heat loss and heat gain
connections.text: The Otipemisiwak Métis Government is the government of the Métis Nation within Alberta. Its head office is on Kingsway Avenue in Edmonton. The City of Edmonton reports that after the Métis Nation of Alberta adopted a climate plan, it audited and retrofitted many of its buildings, upgrading heating and air systems, windows and insulation. In a 2025 survey, many Citizens said they had experienced extreme heat. Its Environment and Climate Change team now sends Heat Response Kits to Citizens aged 60 and up, with an air conditioner, a thermometer and an energy saving kit. Its tips include weather stripping, thermal drapes and closing blinds during the hottest hours.

sources.title: Otipemisiwak Métis Government: About the Otipemisiwak Métis Government (government of the Métis Nation within Alberta; Edmonton head office)
City of Edmonton, Transforming Edmonton: Métis Nation of Alberta Climate Action Plan (energy audits and retrofits: heating and air systems, windows, insulation)
Otipemisiwak Métis Government: Heat Response Program (2025 survey, kit contents, tips for staying cool)

peoples: Plains Cree: Frog Lake First Nations
connections.title: Asinikahtamwak: building blocks that insulate
connections.text: Frog Lake First Nations is a Plains Cree community in Treaty 6 territory, near the Saskatchewan border. It owns 51 per cent of Asinikahtamwak, which CBC says is Cree for "works with rock." An Edmonton company and Elk Point own the rest. Its plant in Elk Point, about 215 km northeast of Edmonton, opened in summer 2024. It makes building blocks from cement, water and hemp fibre. They are the size of cinder blocks but weigh about half as much. The company says the blocks give better thermal insulation. Michael Marty, clean energy manager for Frog Lake First Nations, says the blocks could slow the spread of fire.

sources.title: Source of the name Asinikahtamwak (Cree for "works with rock"), ownership, insulation claim and Michael Marty's words: CBC News, Indigenous-owned Alberta company making better building blocks, with hemp (February 2025)
Frog Lake First Nations: About Frog Lake (Plains Cree; Treaty 6; near the Saskatchewan border)

connections.title: Iglu: snow walls that slow heat transfer
connections.text: In Inuktitut, iglu means "house." The Canadian Encyclopedia says hard snow walls are good insulators that keep in body heat and the heat from oil lamps. Inside, it is often just above freezing and can reach about 15 °C. Chaim Christiana Andersen, writing from her Labrador Inuit family's history, and Geoff Rayner-Canham explain that fresh snow conducts heat more poorly than modern house insulation because of air trapped between crystals. The entrance tunnel is below ground level, and warm air is less dense than cold air, so the inside stays warm. Iqaluit Elder Solomon Awa learned to build igluvigat from his father. Some Elders teach iglu building today.

sources.title: Source of the name iglu (house); snow walls as insulators; inside temperatures; Elders teaching iglu building today: The Canadian Encyclopedia, Igloo

Snow's low thermal conductivity (trapped air) and the low entrance tunnel (warm air less dense): Chaim Christiana Andersen and Geoff Rayner-Canham, University of Waterloo, Chemistry and Inuit Life and Culture: snow making life possible in the Arctic
Source of the word igluvigat and Solomon Awa learning iglu building from his father: CBC News, Building anew on Inuit land

connections.title: SmartICE: measuring a warming sea ice
connections.text: Inuit judge the thickness, strength and snow cover of sea ice with knowledge passed down over generations. CBC reports that the North is warming faster than other regions, and that warmer ocean currents are thinning the ice from underneath. SmartICE, founded in Nain, Nunatsiavut, and St. John's, supports this knowledge rather than replacing it. Its SmartBUOY, set into the ice, measures air, snow, ice and water temperature. Inuit youth trained in Nain build the devices by hand. The buoys go "where the communities tell us to go," says SmartICE leader Carolann Harding. Rex Howell of Nain says of the sea ice: "It's our highway to get to our food."

sources.title: CBC Radio, Quirks and Quarks: SmartICE: Supporting Inuit knowledge of the landscape with technology (2020; Inuit ice knowledge, North warming, Rex Howell's words)
Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency: SmartICE (founded in St. John's and Nain; SmartBUOY temperature readings; Inuit youth program in Nain, Nunatsiavut)
CBC News: SmartICE opens Nain production centre for ice-measuring tech (devices made by hand; Carolann Harding's words)

try: Think of an iglu as a system on a cold night. Name where energy moves by conduction, by convection and by radiation. How do the snow walls with their trapped air, the low entrance tunnel and the oil lamp each change the rate of heat transfer? Compare the snow walls with the foam cup in Investigation 2.

Hemp blocks, attic insulation, weather stripping and thermal drapes all slow heat transfer. For each one, which process does it mainly slow: conduction, convection or radiation? In January, which way does energy move through an Edmonton wall? On a 30 °C summer day, which way does it move? Explain why the same insulation helps in both seasons.

A SmartBUOY measures the temperature of the air, snow, ice and water. Use the Earth's thermostat model and Lesson 6 to explain what happens to the sunlight absorbed in an area when bright sea ice melts and darker open ocean takes its place. Why do Inuit ice knowledge and sensor readings work well together?

slide.title: Snow walls, hemp blocks and sea ice
points: Edmonton: The Otipemisiwak Métis Government retrofits buildings with insulation and helps Citizens stay cool in extreme heat.
Alberta: Frog Lake First Nations is majority owner of Asinikahtamwak, which makes insulating hemp building blocks.
Canada: Iglu snow walls trap air to slow heat transfer, and SmartICE helps Inuit measure warming sea ice.
slide.notes: Use with Lesson 5 (Insulation slows heat transfer) and Lesson 3 (Conduction, convection and radiation). Ask students which process each example slows: trapped air in snow and hemp blocks limits conduction and convection; drapes and closed blinds reduce radiation and drafts. The iglu entrance tunnel links to convection: warm air is less dense than cold air. SmartICE suits Lesson 6 (How the Sun sets Earth's temperature) and Lab Bench Investigation 3 (Earth's thermostat): melting ice means less reflection and more absorption. The Métis and Frog Lake examples also support the Written Review extended response on lowering an Edmonton winter heating bill. Point students to the Ways of knowing section in the lab for sources and discussion prompts.

review_flags: Existing content: I found no Indigenous content in the Temperature and Heating Lab or the deck, sourced or unsourced. The only reference is the footer "Edmonton, Treaty 6 territory." The Coverage tab lists "bison winter coats" and "prairie snow cover" as everyday Alberta contexts with no Indigenous framing.

Building on Energy Accounts: the qulliq appears here only as "oil lamps" inside the iglu, from The Canadian Encyclopedia. I did not repeat the tarquti, the Nunavik wind projects or Alacie Joamie's words. I did not find, in this task, an Inuit-authored source that describes the qulliq in terms of heat transfer, so I did not go deeper. An Inuit Knowledge Keeper (for example through an Edmonton Inuit organization) would be the right person to share more about the qulliq and the iglu.

Names and spellings, with sources: iglu, "house" (The Canadian Encyclopedia); igluvigat (CBC, Building anew on Inuit land, used without translation); Asinikahtamwak, "works with rock" (CBC only; I could not confirm it on a Frog Lake First Nations or company page); Otipemisiwak, which the government's own page translates as "the people who own themselves" (I did not include this translation in the text; add it if you like). Spelling of iglu varies across sources (iglu, igloo, igluit, igluvigaq, igluvigat). I used iglu as the Canadian Encyclopedia and the Waterloo article do. Please confirm.

Inside iglu temperatures differ: The Canadian Encyclopedia says often just above freezing, up to about 15 °C; the Waterloo article uses +20 °C in an example calculation. I used the Encyclopedia's numbers.

Elder title: CBC calls Solomon Awa "an Iqaluit elder and expert igloo-builder" (also now mayor). I capitalized Elder. The Canadian Encyclopedia says "some elders teach building." Please confirm the capitalization you prefer.

Waterloo article authorship: Chaim Christiana Andersen writes from her Labrador Inuit family's history in Okak and Nain; Geoff Rayner-Canham's background is not given on the page. It is a science education article, not an Inuit organization source. Is it acceptable as the main source for the snow conductivity and entrance tunnel facts?

Edmonton connection: the retrofits are described for the Métis Nation of Alberta's buildings in general, not Edmonton buildings specifically. The Edmonton link is the head office and the City of Edmonton source. The Heat Response Program is open to Citizens anywhere in Alberta. The Transforming Edmonton article is undated. The Heat Response page says applications are now closed (round two, 50 kits). Is this connection strong enough for the Edmonton scale, or should it move to Alberta?

Frog Lake: froglake.ca says Plains Cree and mentions Treaty 6 but gives no adhesion date and does not mention Asinikahtamwak. I wrote "Plains Cree" rather than nêhiyaw because no source I fetched for this nation uses nêhiyaw. CBC gives no R value or test data for the insulation claim, so I wrote that "the company says." I avoided Frog Lake's 1885 history on purpose.

SmartICE: I did not call it Inuit-owned or Inuit-led. CBC (2020) says Memorial University geographer Trevor Bell leads the program; the ACOA page (2024) calls Carolann Harding CEO and says the board is 50 per cent Indigenous. CBC (Nain centre story, undated) calls her executive director, so I wrote "SmartICE leader." The ACOA page says SmartICE works in more than 35 Indigenous communities; I left the number out. Pond Inlet is named in the peoples field because CBC names Andrew Arreak, operations lead there; it is not in the text. Please confirm.

Alternative Alberta connection not used: Windspeaker (March 31, 2026) reports the "Lubicon standard" at Lubicon Lake Cree Nation: airtight new homes, about 30 per cent more energy efficient, heat recovery ventilators and backup wood stoves. Tegan Martin-Drysdale, infrastructure project manager, said: "When the power goes out at minus 30 or minus 40, we need to keep everyone warm, so homes now include backup heat sources like wood stoves." Source: https://windspeaker.com/news/windspeaker-news/first-nation-establishes-lubicon-standard-new-climate-resilient-housing-and . It fits convection (airtightness) and radiation (wood stoves). Would you like it added or swapped in?

Not used: a Kitikmeot Heritage Society PDF on iglu building would not load, so I did not cite it. The Canadian Encyclopedia tipi article does not discuss liners or warmth, so I did not use the tipi. Inuit caribou skin clothing as insulation would fit Lesson 5 well, but I did not fetch a Canadian Inuit source on it in this task.

Sensitive topic: the SmartICE connection and the heat program touch on climate change. Both frame communities as acting with knowledge and tools, matching the deck's note to focus on actions rather than doom.

The iglu also appears as the Canada connection in the Structures and Loads Lab draft (g7-f1), where it is taught as a shell structure. Here it is about insulation and convection. Both drafts cite the same Canadian Encyclopedia and CBC pages but use different facts. Is it fine for the iglu to appear in both labs, or should one lab use a different Inuit example (for example Inuit caribou skin clothing, if a good source can be found)?
